title: Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS) #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.1
summary: Republishes version 2.1 of PKCS #1 from RSA Laboratories, covering RSA cryptography including encryption, signatures and encoding methods. Change control stays with the PKCS process, and the text was taken from that document with some corrections. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 8017.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3447 is the written-down rules for using RSA safely. It says how a key is made, how a message is turned into the bytes that get encrypted or signed, and exactly which padding and encoding each scheme uses. Four schemes are defined: two for encrypting a message and two for signing one.

subtitle: The reference specification for RSA encryption and signatures, republished from RSA Laboratories as PKCS #1 v2.1.

tldr.problem: RSA is a single mathematical operation, and applying it to a message safely needs careful rules about padding, key sizes and how the data is laid out before the arithmetic happens.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC builds up from four arithmetic primitives to four complete schemes: OAEP and PKCS #1 v1.5 for encryption, and PSS and PKCS #1 v1.5 for signatures, each combining a primitive with a defined encoding of the message.
tldr.outcome: It is a republication of PKCS #1 v2.1 with change control kept inside the PKCS process, and a few corrections made during publication. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8017.

today: RFC 3447 has been obsoleted by RFC 8017, so it is no longer a current standards document. It was published in February 2003 as an Informational republication of PKCS #1 v2.1, with change control retained inside the PKCS process, and it had itself obsoleted RFC 2437.

sections.title: What PKCS #1 Covers
sections.content:
This document gives recommendations for implementing public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm. It covers cryptographic primitives, encryption schemes, signature schemes with appendix, and the ASN.1 syntax for representing keys and for identifying the schemes.

The recommendations are intended for general use within computer and communications systems and so include a fair amount of flexibility. Application standards built on these specifications may add their own constraints. The recommendations are intended to be compatible with IEEE-1363-2000 and with the drafts then being developed by the ANSI X9F1 and IEEE P1363 working groups. This document supersedes PKCS #1 version 2.0 but includes compatible techniques.

The document is organised from the bottom up. Section 2 defines the notation. Section 3 defines the RSA public and private key types. Sections 4 and 5 define primitives, that is, basic mathematical operations: data conversion primitives in Section 4, and cryptographic primitives for encryption and decryption and for signature and verification in Section 5. Sections 6 to 8 deal with the schemes built on those primitives: an overview, then an OAEP-based encryption scheme, then a PSS-based signature scheme with appendix, alongside the methods from PKCS #1 v1.5. Section 9 defines the encoding methods the signature schemes use. The appendices give the ASN.1 syntax, the hash functions and the mask generation function, an ASN.1 module, intellectual property considerations, the revision history, references and general information about the Public-Key Cryptography Standards.

The RFC itself is a republication of PKCS #1 v2.1 from RSA Laboratories, with change control retained inside the PKCS process. The body is taken directly from the PKCS #1 v2.1 document with certain corrections made during the publication process, and an appendix lists those corrections.
sections.plainLanguage: It reads like a reference manual, from the arithmetic up to complete algorithms, because the safety of RSA depends on every layer agreeing. It was published as an RFC so that the specification had a stable, citable form.

sections.title: Key Types and Data Conversion
sections.content:
Two key types are used throughout: the RSA public key and the RSA private key, which together form an RSA key pair. The specification supports so-called multi-prime RSA, where the modulus may have more than two prime factors. The benefit is a lower computational cost for the decryption and signature primitives, provided the Chinese Remainder Theorem is used. Better performance can be achieved on single processor platforms, and to a greater extent on multiprocessor platforms, where the modular exponentiations involved can be done in parallel.

An RSA public key has two components: the modulus n, a positive integer, and the public exponent e, a positive integer. In a valid public key, n is a product of u distinct odd primes r_i, where u is at least 2, and e is an integer between 3 and n minus 1 satisfying GCD(e, lambda(n)) = 1, where lambda(n) is the least common multiple of r_1 minus 1 and so on. By convention the first two primes may also be called p and q.

The private key has two possible representations. The first is the pair (n, d), where d is the private exponent, a positive integer less than n satisfying e times d equal to 1 modulo lambda(n). The second is a quintuple (p, q, dP, dQ, qInv) together with a possibly empty sequence of triplets (r_i, d_i, t_i), one for each prime not in the quintuple. The CRT exponents dP and dQ satisfy e times dP equal to 1 modulo p minus 1 and e times dQ equal to 1 modulo q minus 1, and the CRT coefficient qInv satisfies q times qInv equal to 1 modulo p.

One note explains an oddity: the definitions of the CRT coefficients and the formulas that use them follow Garner's algorithm, but for compatibility with the key representations in PKCS #1 v2.0 and earlier versions the roles of p and q are reversed compared to the rest of the primes, so the first CRT coefficient qInv is the inverse of q modulo p rather than the inverse of p modulo q.

Two data conversion primitives move between integers and byte strings. I2OSP converts a nonnegative integer to an octet string of a specified length, failing with the error integer too large if the integer does not fit. OS2IP converts an octet string to a nonnegative integer by reading it as base 256 digits. An octet string is an ordered sequence of eight-bit bytes indexed from first to last, and for these conversions the first octet is the most significant.
sections.plainLanguage: An RSA key is a big number and a small exponent, with the big number secretly built from primes. The private key can be stored either as the exponent alone or as the separate pieces needed to work with each prime in turn, which is faster. Everything else in the document turns messages into numbers and back again.

sections.title: The Four Cryptographic Primitives
sections.content:
Cryptographic primitives are the basic mathematical operations that schemes are built from. They are intended for implementation in hardware or as software modules, and are not intended to provide security apart from a scheme. Four types are specified, organised in pairs: encryption and decryption, and signature and verification. The specifications assume that certain conditions are met by the inputs, in particular that the RSA keys are valid.

The encryption primitive RSAEP takes the public key and a message representative, an integer between 0 and n minus 1, and produces a ciphertext representative by computing c = m to the power e modulo n. If the message representative is outside that range it reports message representative out of range. The decryption primitive RSADP takes the private key and a ciphertext representative and recovers the message representative. It is the same mathematical operation with the private exponent in place of the public one, and the private key may be given in either of its two representations, in which case the Chinese Remainder Theorem is used.

The signature primitive RSASP1 takes the private key and a message representative and produces a signature representative, again by exponentiation with the private exponent. The verification primitive RSAVP1 takes the public key and a signature representative and produces a message representative by raising it to the power e modulo n, so verification uses only the public key.

The primitives specified here are the same as IFEP-RSA and IFDP-RSA in IEEE Std 1363-2000, except that support for multi-prime RSA has been added, and they are compatible with PKCS #1 v1.5.
sections.plainLanguage: All four primitives are the same operation, a modular exponentiation. Encrypt and sign with the private key; decrypt and verify with the public one. Everything else in the document is about preparing the data before that operation and checking it afterwards.

sections.title: Encryption Schemes
sections.content:
An encryption scheme consists of an encryption operation, which produces a ciphertext from a message using the recipient's RSA public key, and a decryption operation, which recovers the message using the corresponding private key. A typical application is a key establishment protocol, where the message carries key material to be delivered confidentially from one party to another. PKCS #7, for instance, uses such a protocol to deliver a content-encryption key from a sender to a recipient, and the schemes here would be suitable key-encryption algorithms in that context.

Two encryption schemes are specified. RSAES-OAEP is recommended for new applications. RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 is included only for compatibility with existing applications and is not recommended for new ones.

Both follow a general model: the encryption operation applies a message encoding operation to the message to produce an encoded message, which is converted to an integer message representative, and the encryption primitive turns that into the ciphertext. Decryption reverses this. To avoid implementation weaknesses in the way errors are handled inside the decoding operation, the encoding and decoding steps are embedded in the specifications of the two schemes rather than defined separately.

RSAES-OAEP combines the RSAEP and RSADP primitives with the EME-OAEP encoding method, which is based on Bellare and Rogaway's Optimal Asymmetric Encryption scheme; OAEP stands for Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding. It can operate on messages of length up to k minus 2hLen minus 2 octets, where hLen is the length of the hash output and k is the length in octets of the recipient's RSA modulus. Assuming that computing e-th roots modulo n is infeasible and that the mask generation function has appropriate properties, the scheme is semantically secure against adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks, and the difficulty of breaking it can be related directly to the difficulty of inverting RSA, provided the mask generation function is viewed as a black box or random oracle. Both encryption and decryption take a label as input, and in this version of PKCS #1 the label is the empty string. The scheme is parameterised by the choice of hash function and mask generation function, and that choice should be fixed for a given RSA key.

RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 encodes the message as a zero octet, a 0x02 octet, a string of pseudo-randomly generated non-zero octets, a zero octet and the message itself, and the message may be at most k minus 11 octets long. The RFC attaches security recommendations: the pseudo-random octets should be generated independently for each encryption, the padding string should be at least eight octets long, and the pseudo-random octets help thwart an attack on low-exponent RSA when similar messages are encrypted with the same key. It is also possible to generate valid RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 ciphertexts without knowing the plaintext, with a reasonable probability of success, and that ability can be exploited in a chosen-ciphertext attack; the RFC's countermeasures include adding structure to the data being encoded, checking PKCS #1 v1.5 conformance carefully in decrypted messages, and consolidating error messages in a client-server protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the arithmetic runs, the message has to be reshaped into a block of exactly the right length, and the reshaping has to be done in a way that does not leak anything. The recommended method mixes in random bytes and a hash, so that the block looks the same whatever the message was.

sections.title: Signature Schemes
sections.content:
RSASSA-PSS combines the RSASP1 and RSAVP1 primitives with the EMSA-PSS encoding method, and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 combines the same two primitives with the EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 encoding method. RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 is compatible with the IFSSA scheme of IEEE Std 1363-2000. The length of messages on which RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 can operate is either unrestricted or constrained by a very large number, depending on the hash function underlying its encoding method.

Assuming that computing e-th roots modulo n is infeasible and that the hash function has appropriate properties, RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 is conjectured to provide secure signatures: forging signatures without knowing the RSA private key is conjectured to be computationally infeasible. Because a hash function identifier is embedded in the encoding, an adversary trying to find a message with the same signature as a previously signed message must find collisions of that particular hash function, and attacking a different hash function is not useful.

The EMSA-PSS encoding hashes the message, prepends eight zero octets and appends a random salt, hashes that again, and builds the encoded message from a masked data block, the second hash and a trailing 0xbc octet. The data block is masked with a mask derived from the second hash, and the leftmost bits of the first octet are set to zero so that the encoded message never exceeds the modulus. Typical salt lengths are hLen and 0.

The signature operation converts the encoded message to an integer, applies the RSASP1 primitive with the private key, and converts the result to a signature of length k octets. Verification converts the signature back to an integer, applies RSAVP1 with the public key, converts the result back to an encoded message, and then checks that the encoded message is consistent with the message. The output is either valid signature or invalid signature.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing here means building a block of bytes from the message and a random salt, and then raising that block to the private exponent. Verification raises the signature to the public exponent instead and checks that the same block comes back. The random salt is what stops one signature being reused for a different message.

sections.title: Scope, Key Management and the One-Key Rule
sections.content:
The RFC's own Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are discussed throughout the memo. The most important of those discussions is in Section 6, on what the schemes do and do not cover.

A scheme combines cryptographic primitives and other techniques to achieve a particular security goal, and the schemes here are limited in scope: their operations consist only of steps to process data with an RSA public or private key, and they do not include steps for obtaining or validating the key. An application will typically add key management operations of its own, and the behaviour of an implementation is unspecified when a key is invalid. The RFC lists three ways of addressing that, including explicit validation by the application, validation within the public-key infrastructure, and assigning liability for operations performed with an invalid key to the party who generated the key.

The section then gives advice that is easy to miss: a generally good cryptographic practice is to employ a given RSA key pair in only one scheme, because a vulnerability in one scheme could then compromise the other, and because it may be essential to maintain provable security. While RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 have traditionally been used together without any known bad interactions, that combined use is not recommended for new applications. The reasoning is given as an example: if the same key pair were used in RSAES-OAEP and RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5, then although OAEP by itself would resist attack, an opponent might exploit a weakness in the implementation of RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 to recover messages encrypted under either scheme. Likewise, a key pair used in both RSASSA-PSS and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 would leave the security proof for PSS insufficient, because the proof does not account for the possibility of signatures being generated with a second scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: These rules cover the arithmetic and the padding, not the handling of keys. The sharpest warning is to use a different key pair for each scheme, because a flaw in the older padding scheme could otherwise be reached through the newer one.

items.label: Encryption
items.desc: c = m^e mod n. Turns a message representative into a ciphertext representative using the public key.

items.label: Decryption
items.desc: Recovers the message representative from the ciphertext representative using the private key, optionally through the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

items.label: Signing
items.desc: s = m^d mod n. Turns a message representative into a signature representative using the private key.

items.label: Verification
items.desc: m = s^e mod n. Recovers the message representative from the signature using the public key only.

data.title: Encoded message structures
data.code:
EME-PKCS1-v1_5:  EM = 0x00 || 0x02 || PS || 0x00 || M
                PS = k - mLen - 3 pseudo-random non-zero octets

EME-OAEP:         EM = 0x00 || maskedSeed || maskedDB
                DB = lHash || PS || 0x01 || M
                maskedDB = DB XOR dbMask
                dbMask = MGF(seed, k - hLen - 1)
                maskedSeed = seed XOR MGF(maskedDB, hLen)

EMSA-PSS:         EM = maskedDB || H || 0xbc
                DB = PS || 0x01 || salt
                maskedDB = DB XOR MGF(H, emLen - hLen - 1)
